 She Is 72 and Struggling to Buy Groceries on Her $700 Social Security Check. As Food Insecurity Nearly Doubles Among Seniors, She Could Qualify for Hundreds More Per Month
 Gerelyn Terzo Fri, November 13, 2026 at 6:36 PM CST 6 min read Quick Read 
 Seniors with tiny Social Security checks can also collect Supplemental Security Income, which could add roughly $349 monthly to a $700 benefit. 
 Food insecurity among Americans 65 and older nearly doubled to 17%, while senior-specific inflation outpaces the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment. 
 Applicants generally need under $2,000 in countable savings, excluding a home and one vehicle, and SSI pays nothing for months before applying.

 Picture a 72-year-old woman who lives alone, gets a Social Security deposit of $700 a month, and has started putting items back at the grocery checkout. She is hypothetical, but plenty of real retirees are in her spot. A November 4 survey from Dunnhumby found that food insecurity among Americans 65 and older nearly doubled, reaching 17%. That figure counts seniors who reported going without enough food. It does not measure how many qualify for any program. 
 Moyo Studio / E+ via Getty Images Rising prices explain part of the pressure. A research inflation index that tracks spending by households led by someone 62 or older rose 3.9% over the past year, while the Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 is 3.6%. On a small check, even a narrow gap like that shows up in the grocery cart. 
 Many people in her position never hear about a second federal program that may owe them money every month. 
 Why a Retirement Check Doesn't Close the Door on SSI 
 Supplemental Security Income, called SSI, is a separate federal program for adults 65 and older with very limited income and savings. It is paid for out of general tax revenue, so she doesn't need a work record to qualify.

 She can collect both at once. Social Security counts as income when the agency figures an SSI payment, so it reduces the SSI amount, but it doesn't disqualify her. Think of SSI as a way to supplement very low income, provided she meets the program's other requirements. 
 Story Continues How Her Income Could Climb by $349 a Month 
 The maximum federal SSI payment for an individual is $1,029 a month in 2027, up from $994 in 2026. Assume her $700 Social Security benefit is her only income in 2027. Here is the rough math: 
 SSI generally ignores the first $20 of her monthly Social Security income. That brings her countable income down to $680. 
 Subtract that from the $1,029 maximum, and the gap is $349. That gap is her potential SSI payment. 
 Her combined federal benefits rise to $1,049 a month, which works out to $4,188 more over a year. 
 One detail surprises people. Once SSI is in the picture, every Social Security dollar above that $20 exclusion cuts SSI by a dollar. A smaller retirement check generally means a bigger SSI payment, and a bigger check means a smaller one, keeping the combined amount roughly the same. 
 SSI can also unlock help beyond the check itself. In most states, SSI recipients qualify for Medicaid, which can cover the Medicare Part B premium of $202.90 a month in 2026 that's normally taken out of Social Security (that premium is only the opening bid on Medicare's real cost, something we mapped out in a free guide to the program's hidden bills). There is a catch, though. If her $700 is what's left after that premium comes out, the agency will count her higher benefit before deductions, so her SSI payment would come in lower than $349. 
 A $2,000 Savings Cap Decides Who Gets In 
 Income is only half the test. A single applicant generally can't have more than $2,000 in countable resources. That includes cash, bank accounts and investments. 
 A lot of what she has probably doesn't count. Her home and the land under it, household goods, one vehicle used for transportation and burial spaces are all excluded. So are life insurance policies with a combined face value of $1,500 or less. 
 Four other factors can change her eligibility or her payment: 
 Marriage. Couples face a $1,544 federal maximum and a $3,000 resource limit. A spouse's income and savings count too. 
 Living arrangements. If she lives in someone else's home and receives free shelter, her SSI payment can go down. 
 Other income. A small pension, annuity or regular cash help from family counts against SSI the same way her Social Security does. 
 State supplements. Some states add their own payment on top of the federal amount, which can push her total above $1,049. 
 Steps Worth Taking Before Assuming There's No Help 
 Waiting is the costliest mistake. SSI generally starts the month after she applies and doesn't pay for the months before that. Every month she spends wondering whether she qualifies is money she won't get back. She can apply by phone or at a local Social Security office and bring bank statements, her benefit letter and any insurance policies. 
 She should also be careful with any savings above the limit. Spending money on things she actually needs is fine, but giving it away to get under $2,000 can lead to a penalty period with no SSI. Have that conversation with the agency or a legal aid office before moving any money. 
 Her small Social Security check may not be all the monthly help she's entitled to. Her exact amount will depend on details like her state, her housing and what she has in the bank, so the answer for her could differ a bit from the example here. Checking costs nothing, and it could mean several hundred dollars more each month for groceries.
